description: Recognition and interpretation of common atrial arrhythmias
overview: This module covers the identification and clinical significance of atrial arrhythmias including atrial fibrillation, atrial flutter, and atrial tachycardia.
objectives: Distinguish atrial tachycardia from sinus tachycardia
Understand clinical implications of atrial arrhythmias
prerequisites: Module 3: Heart Rate and Rhythm Analysis

slides.title: Atrial Fibrillation
slides.content: Atrial fibrillation: irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, fibrillatory waves, variable R-R intervals. Risk of thromboembolism. Most common sustained arrhythmia in adults. May be paroxysmal, persistent, or permanent.

slides.title: Atrial Flutter
slides.content: Atrial flutter: sawtooth pattern (flutter waves), regular atrial rate ~300 bpm, variable ventricular response. Usually 2:1, 3:1, or 4:1 conduction. May degenerate to atrial fibrillation.

quiz.question: What is the characteristic pattern of atrial flutter?
quiz.explanation: Atrial flutter is characterized by a sawtooth pattern of flutter waves.

slides.title: Atrial Tachycardia
slides.content: Atrial tachycardia: regular rhythm, P waves present but abnormal morphology, rate >100 bpm, 1:1 AV conduction. May be caused by enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, or reentry.

quiz.question: What distinguishes atrial tachycardia from sinus tachycardia?
quiz.explanation: Atrial tachycardia has abnormal P wave morphology compared to normal sinus P waves.

slides.title: Clinical Management
slides.content: Management considerations: rate vs rhythm control, anticoagulation for stroke prevention, underlying cause identification. Emergency management for unstable patients includes cardioversion.

quiz.question: What is the primary concern in atrial fibrillation management?
quiz.explanation: Stroke prevention through anticoagulation is the primary concern in atrial fibrillation management.
